The central question is whether the two leading methods for modifying internal representations in neural networks — activation steering (adding a vector to residual stream activations at inference time) and representation engineering (training a linear probe to read/write along a concept direction, typically with a contrast-pair dataset) — suppress different subsets of features when they target a polysemantic neuron or direction, even when their behavioral outputs look identical. A polysemantic neuron encodes multiple unrelated concepts superimposed in the same weights; any intervention that pushes along one concept's direction will geometrically interfere with other concepts sharing that subspace, but the degree and identity of collateral suppression likely differs by modality because the two methods find different "concept directions" through different optimization pressures. The expert worry that beginners miss is this: behavioral equivalence is not mechanistic equivalence — two interventions can produce the same output token distribution while one is silencing three latent features and the other is silencing one, meaning downstream interpretability conclusions (e.g., "this neuron implements safety-relevant concept X") will be intervention-artifact-dependent rather than ground truth. Concretely, activation steering typically adds a fixed vector derived from a small paired prompt set, which may sit at an angle to the true feature direction and project energy into neighboring features in superposition; representation engineering's contrast-consistent direction may track the principal axis of a concept more faithfully but introduces its own bias from the choice of contrast pairs. The practical danger is that researchers comparing "what features are suppressed when we ablate concept X" across labs using different modalities are measuring partly different things and may publish contradictory mechanistic claims without realizing the intervention methodology is the hidden variable.

The cleanest measurement is to read out the activation magnitudes of other known features — ideally sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents — on held-out prompts that probe those co-encoded concepts, comparing across the two intervention conditions against an unintervened baseline. Anthropic's published SAE work on Claude (Templeton et al. 2024) demonstrated that individual SAE latents can be interpreted as monosemantic feature detectors with high specificity; if you run both interventions and then project residual stream activations onto the SAE dictionary, you get a per-latent activation vector and can directly compute which latents were suppressed by how much under each modality — a suppression profile in ~tens-of-thousands-dimensional latent space rather than just behavioral output. The critical experimental control is a feature specificity ratio: for each intervention, measure suppression on target-concept latents versus suppression on semantically unrelated latents that happen to co-activate with the target neuron; a well-targeted intervention should have a high ratio, and the two modalities will almost certainly differ on this ratio even when matched on behavioral suppression of X. Nanda et al.'s work on superposition in toy models gives you a synthetic ground truth version of this — you can construct a model where you know which features are superimposed, apply both interventions, and directly verify the collateral damage against the known dictionary rather than an inferred one. The number to watch for is whether collateral suppression exceeds ~10-15% of baseline latent activation magnitude for unrelated features, since below that threshold the effect is plausibly noise, but above it you have evidence of genuine geometric crosstalk that differs by intervention modality.

The core strategy is triangulation across multiple independent measurement instruments: if two SAEs trained with different sparsity penalties (say, L1 coefficient 1e-3 versus 5e-3), different widths (e.g., 4x versus 32x expansion), and different architectures (standard ReLU SAE versus Anthropic's gated SAE variant) all agree that intervention A suppresses latent cluster Y more than intervention B does, the finding is unlikely to be an artifact of any single SAE's geometry. Concretely, you'd compute the Jaccard similarity between the sets of "significantly suppressed latents" across SAE variants for each intervention modality — high Jaccard within a modality and low Jaccard across modalities is the signal you want; if instead Jaccard is low within a modality across SAE variants, you have an SAE-dependency problem that undermines the whole comparison. A second orthogonal check is to bypass SAEs entirely and use probing classifiers trained on activations to detect the co-encoded features: if a linear probe for feature Z (trained before any intervention) shows depressed confidence under intervention A but not B, that suppression signal comes from the raw activation geometry rather than any SAE decomposition, and convergence between probe results and SAE results is strong evidence against measurement artifact. A third check exploits causal intervention logic directly — patch in activations from a prompt that strongly activates the suspected collaterally-suppressed feature and measure whether the intervention still suppresses behavioral expression of that feature; this is a causal rather than correlational test that requires no learned dictionary at all. The uncomfortable residual worry is that all these methods share the assumption that linear structure captures the relevant features, so a finding that survives all three checks could still be an artifact of the linearity assumption rather than genuine suppression — but at that point you've exhausted the current methodological toolkit and the burden shifts to critics to propose a nonlinear measurement that would change the conclusion.

The naive implication — representation engineering is safer because it causes less collateral suppression — is probably wrong in the alignment-critical context, and here's why: collateral suppression of unrelated features might actually be desirable if those features are themselves hazardous, meaning a blunter instrument that suppresses more could be better from a safety standpoint depending entirely on the valence of the collaterally suppressed content. "Safer" in ordinary usage means something like "fewer unintended side effects," but in alignment-critical interventions it should mean "lower probability of model behavior that violates intended constraints," and those two definitions come apart precisely when the unintended side effects happen to suppress dangerous capabilities — a point Zou et al.'s representation engineering paper (2023) gestures at but doesn't resolve, because they evaluate behavioral outcomes rather than the mechanistic suppression profile. The deeper problem is that alignment-critical interventions require predictability above all else: a more targeted intervention that suppresses only concept X is more predictable in its effects, while a blunter one that also suppresses Y and Z introduces uncertainty about what else changed, and unpredictability is arguably the central failure mode in deployed safety interventions even when the immediate behavior looks correct. Concretely, consider an intervention targeting deceptive reasoning: if activation steering collaterally suppresses general planning capacity by 20% (a plausible number given the geometric argument about superposition) while representation engineering suppresses it by 3%, the steering intervention might produce a model that appears less deceptive partly because it's less capable of coherent multi-step reasoning — a Goodhart's Law failure where you've optimized the behavioral metric without addressing the underlying feature. So the correct framing is not "which modality is safer" but "which modality's collateral suppression profile is auditable and predictable," and that demands exactly the SAE-based and probe-based measurement infrastructure from the previous turn — without it, neither modality deserves the label "safe" in any technically meaningful sense.

The mathematical requirement is that the intervention vector lie within the span of the target feature's dictionary atoms while being orthogonal to all other feature directions you want to preserve — formally, if you have an SAE dictionary matrix D with columns d_1...d_n, and your target is d_t, the ideal intervention vector v must satisfy v·d_i ≈ 0 for all i≠t, which is only achievable without approximation error if d_t is linearly independent of every other feature you care about preserving. In practice, superposition means features are not orthogonal — Elhage et al. (2022) showed that a model storing k features in n<k dimensions will pack them at angles of roughly arccos(1/√n) apart, meaning perfect confinement is geometrically impossible, but you can construct a least-collateral-damage vector by solving a constrained optimization: minimize ||v - d_t||² subject to |v·d_i| < ε for a chosen tolerance ε across the m features you most want to preserve. This is essentially a projection problem — project d_t onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the m protected features — and the residual after projection is your best achievable confined intervention vector; the norm of the discarded component tells you directly how much target-feature suppression you're sacrificing to achieve collateral protection, giving you an explicit precision-collateral tradeoff curve rather than a binary choice. The practical obstacle is that you need a sufficiently complete and accurate feature dictionary to enumerate the protected subspace, and current SAEs at the scales relevant for alignment (Claude-level models) likely miss many features — Anthropic's work suggests their largest published SAEs recover perhaps 20-40% of explainable variance in MLP layers, meaning the orthogonal complement you're projecting onto is incomplete and your "confined" vector will still have unaudited collateral effects in the unrecovered subspace. A further constraint that's easy to miss: the intervention must remain confined not just at the layer where it's applied but through subsequent transformer layers, since residual stream vectors are processed by attention and MLP blocks that rotate and mix the representation — a vector orthogonal to protected features at layer L may not be orthogonal to their transformed versions at layer L+3, so confinement requires either layer-specific re-projection or a theory of how feature directions propagate forward through the network.

The honest answer is that current mechanistic interpretability is implicitly committed to a layer-local notion of feature identity, and the field has not yet reconciled this with the cross-layer analysis that intervention design requires — SAEs are trained independently at each layer, and there is no enforced correspondence between a "deception" latent at layer 14 and whatever direction encodes deception-relevant information at layer 20, even though the behavioral concept presumably persists. Residual stream geometry complicates this further: because transformers use additive residual connections, the stream at layer L is literally the sum of all previous layer outputs, so a feature direction at layer L+1 is not a rotation of the layer-L feature but rather the layer-L feature plus the delta contributed by the layer-L attention and MLP blocks — meaning the same semantic concept may be encoded in geometrically drifting directions as you move through the network, not because the concept changed but because the representational basis is being continuously updated. Some empirical evidence for partial stability exists: Lindsey et al. and related work on cross-layer superposition suggest that certain high-salience features (e.g., token identity, syntactic role) maintain roughly consistent linear readout directions across many layers, with cosine similarities between same-concept probes at adjacent layers often above 0.7 — but this drops sharply for abstract semantic features, which appear to be re-encoded substantially at each major processing stage. The intervention design implication is severe: if you construct your confined intervention vector at layer L using the local SAE dictionary, then propagate it forward, the vector's projection onto the layer L+5 feature dictionary is undefined without a cross-layer correspondence map, and you cannot make confinement guarantees downstream without one. What would actually be needed is something like a feature trajectory — tracking how a concept's encoding direction evolves layer by layer — which requires either a cross-layer SAE with shared dictionary atoms (not yet standard practice) or a learned alignment between per-layer dictionaries, neither of which exists at production scale.

Yes, intervention locus is categorically important, and the difference is not merely quantitative — early-layer interventions operate on representations that are closer to token-level surface features and will be processed and potentially corrected by all subsequent attention and MLP blocks, while late-layer interventions operate on representations that are closer to output distributions and bypass most of the network's subsequent computation, meaning the two act through fundamentally different causal pathways even when their behavioral outputs match. The early-layer intervention faces what you might call the "error correction" problem: transformer MLP blocks have been shown (Geva et al. 2022, "Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Build Predictions by Promoting Concepts in the Residual Stream") to function partly as associative memories that reinstate concept-consistent information, so an intervention that suppresses a feature at layer 5 may be partially undone by layers 6-15 reinstating semantically related content — behavioral suppression at the output then requires the intervention to be strong enough to overcome this correction pressure, which typically means more collateral damage to survive the network's internal dynamics. Late-layer interventions avoid the correction problem but introduce a different failure mode: they suppress the expression of a concept at the output stage without touching the underlying computation that generated it, meaning the model has fully processed and represented the dangerous content internally and only the final readout is blocked — analogous to a person who thinks something dangerous but is prevented from saying it, where the thought still influences latent state. Empirically, Li et al.'s inference-time intervention (ITI) work found that truth-relevant directions were most causally influential at middle-to-late layers (roughly layers 15-20 in a 32-layer model), suggesting the network has a natural "commitment point" where semantic content stabilizes before output projection — intervening near this point may offer the best tradeoff between avoiding error correction and actually affecting the underlying representation rather than just the readout. The reliability asymmetry matters most for adversarial robustness: an early-layer intervention that relies on downstream correction pressure not overcoming it is fragile to prompt perturbations that shift which correction circuits activate, while a late-layer intervention that only blocks output is fragile to any pathway that routes the concept to behavior through non-standard circuits, and neither fragility is visible from behavioral evaluation alone.

Yes, a correction threshold almost certainly exists and is prompt-dependent for a precise mechanistic reason: the strength of MLP reinstatement depends on how strongly the prompt context activates the associative memory keys corresponding to the suppressed feature, so a prompt that richly instantiates the concept's semantic neighborhood will drive stronger correction than a minimal or out-of-distribution prompt, meaning the same intervention vector can be simultaneously above threshold (effectively suppressive) on sparse prompts and below threshold (silently ineffective) on semantically dense ones. The silent ineffectiveness failure mode is particularly dangerous because standard behavioral evaluation uses a finite prompt distribution that may undersample exactly the dense semantic contexts where correction pressure is highest — a model evaluated on 1000 held-out prompts could show 95% behavioral suppression while having near-zero mechanistic suppression on a class of deployment prompts that weren't in the eval set, and you'd never know from the behavioral numbers alone. Detection before deployment requires measuring intervention effectiveness not at the output layer but at the layer immediately after the intervention point: if you apply an intervention at layer L and then measure the target feature's SAE latent activation at layer L+3 versus layer L, a large reinstatement ratio (say, recovery of more than 30-40% of baseline activation) is a direct signal that correction pressure is overcoming the intervention for that prompt. A more scalable detection method is to construct a "semantic stress test" prompt distribution by deliberately maximizing context richness for the target concept — using the model's own internals to find prompts that most strongly activate the target feature pre-intervention, then checking whether intervention effectiveness degrades monotonically with pre-intervention activation strength, which would directly characterize the correction threshold as a function of prompt-induced feature salience. The deeper architectural point is that this failure mode is structurally invisible to any evaluation methodology that treats the model as a black box, which means it cannot be detected by standard red-teaming or capability evaluations and requires the kind of internal activation monitoring infrastructure that almost no deployment pipeline currently implements — making it arguably the highest-priority gap between current interpretability research and deployment-ready alignment tooling.
